chief_complaint: unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus
hpi_details: A 77-year-old male presents to the clinic with unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks deep, impacted earwax or fluid trapped behind his eardrum from an old cold is blocking his hearing.
concerns: He is worried that the sudden ringing and hearing loss are early warning signs of an impending stroke.
expectations: He hopes the doctor can flush his ear canal clean or prescribe targeted drops to clear the blockage.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acoustic Neuroma (Vestibular Schwannoma) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acoustic Neuroma (Vestibular Schwannoma) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Acoustic Neuroma: Brain MRI with IAC protocol, serial scans vs surgery/Gamma Knife, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acoustic Neuroma (Vestibular Schwannoma).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Meniere's disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Facial numbness.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: Is the hearing loss only on one side?
Do you have ringing in that ear?
How long has this been progressing?

history.answer: My right ear has been gradually losing its hearing over the past few months, and there is a constant ringing sound in that ear.
It started about four or five months ago as a subtle hiss and faint muffling, but it has become progressively worse over time.
It is only in my right ear. My left ear hears completely normally.
I really struggle to hear phone calls when holding the phone to my right ear, and I have a hard time understanding people in noisy rooms.
Yes, my right ear feels somewhat plugged or full, almost like there is cotton stuffed deep inside.
It is a continuous high-pitched ringing noise in my right ear. It stays steady and does not pulse with my heartbeat.
The room does not spin, but I have felt slightly unsteady on my feet lately, especially when walking down the hallway in the dark.
No, I have not had any ear pain, fluid drainage, or bleeding from either ear.
No, I have not had a recent cold, stuffy nose, or flu, and I have not flown on a plane or gone diving.
No, I never stick cotton swabs into my ears, and this did not start after showering or swimming.
I have noticed a faint numbness and tingling around my right cheek over the past few weeks, but my face has not drooped.
No, I have not had any severe headaches, weakness in my arms or legs, visual changes, or trouble speaking.
No, I was a schoolteacher, so I was never exposed to loud industrial machinery, gunfire, or loud headphones.
No, I have never received chemotherapy, strong IV antibiotics, or taken large doses of aspirin or water pills.
No, I have never had any head injuries, concussions, or blows to my ears.
No, I never had recurrent ear infections as a child, and I have never had surgery on my ears.
No one in my family had hearing loss at a young age, nerve tumors, or genetic hearing problems.
It has made social gatherings stressful, so I have been avoiding dinners with friends, and I feel tired trying to follow conversations.
Yes, I have felt generally fatigued and drained lately, probably from constantly straining to listen and keep my balance.
I figured it was just stubborn earwax impacted deep inside or fluid left over from a recent cold.
I'm really worried this sudden ringing and muffled hearing mean I'm having mini-strokes.
I was hoping you could just flush my ear out today or give me some powerful ear drops to clear whatever is clogging it.
I have been quite healthy my whole life and have no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, or stroke.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only have an occasional glass of wine once or twice a month at family celebrations.
I am a retired high school teacher and live comfortably at home with my wife.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.6°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
Alert, oriented, well-groomed 77-year-old male in no acute distress.
Bilateral external auditory canals clear without cerumen; tympanic membranes intact, translucent, with normal light reflex and no middle ear fluid.
Whisper test demonstrates reduced acuity on the right side; Weber test lateralizes to the left ear; Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally.
Decreased light touch and pinprick sensation in right V2 and V3 distribution; corneal reflex slightly decreased on the right; facial motor function symmetric without weakness.
Finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements normal; Romberg test reveals mild swaying to the right with eyes closed; tandem gait mildly unsteady.
No spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus; Dix-Hallpike maneuver negative bilaterally with no vertigo or induced nystagmus.
